ca_bayou_aka_the_graveyard_the.blurb: A boulder-filled corner of an old granite quarry inside Deer Creek Park in Rocklin, northeast of Sacramento. The problems sit at the foot of a cliff roughly 20 feet tall, so landings and heights are modest. Most of the 27 problems fall between V0 and V4, with a handful of harder lines stretching toward V10. Cracks, slabs and short traverses make up much of the menu. The pit is shaded for most of the day, which helps on warm afternoons, but the Central Valley summers are hot, so mornings are the better bet then. Expect some litter and a rough urban-park feel; it is an easy, quick session spot for locals.

ca_warning_signs.blurb: A sport wall above a talus slope on the Lower Gorge side of the Owens River Gorge, a short drive from Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. Of its 27 routes, nearly all are bolted, with a few trad lines mixed in. Grades cluster at 5.10 and 5.11, with a smaller number of easier pitches and one or two at 5.12. Pitches run long, roughly 90 to 200 feet, and the rock is generally solid with reliable holds. This is one of the most popular walls in the Lower Gorge, yet the gorge as a whole is less crowded than many Eastern Sierra destinations. Most routes lack lowering stations, so plan on walking off down the talus.

ca_tioga_wall.blurb: A stacked, southeast-facing granite cliff at about 9,000 feet in Lee Vining Canyon, the first big wall you meet dropping east from Tioga Pass. It offers 27 routes, mostly bolted with a few gear lines, and the difficulty is firmly in the upper range: a couple of 5.10s, then mostly 5.11 and 5.12, with a few 5.13s. Lines are long, so bring a long rope, and not every sport route has fixed draws. The wall goes into shade around early afternoon in midsummer. Thin air and quick-changing mountain weather mean this is a place for strong, self-sufficient parties rather than beginners.
ca_tioga_wall.parking_note: Leave the car at a roadside pullout on Highway 120 about 8.2 miles above its junction with US 395, just beyond the green bridge. An old interpretive display near the pullout helps confirm you have the right spot.
ca_tioga_wall.approach: From the pullout, step over the guardrail and follow the steep climbers' path down the canyon on the up-canyon side. The first routes are roughly ten minutes away, and the farthest walls take twenty to twenty-five.

ca_upper_tier_2.blurb: The upper shelf of the South Face of Trapper Dome, a granite dome above Courtright Reservoir in the southern Sierra at roughly 8,500 feet. Around 27 routes begin from a single ledge on a large face, a mix of trad, sport and top-rope lines, many of them multi-pitch in feel. Difficulty runs from a few easy 5.3 to 5.5 lines through a few moderates up to a dense run of 5.10 and 5.11 climbs, with several 5.12s at the top end. Some routes are runout, so it suits parties comfortable placing gear and managing risk. The dome is one of the few spots at the reservoir where you might share the rock with others.

ca_turlock.blurb: A large, popular boulder on the southeast side of Stoney Point Park in Chatsworth, in the San Fernando Valley north of Los Angeles. Its 27 problems cover every face and span the full range, from very easy warm-ups through the middle grades to a few hard problems in the V7 to V9 range. The fine-grained sandstone is kind to skin but brittle, so holds can snap and the rock is best left alone when damp. Glued anchors on top allow top-roping. Summers are hot, so cooler months and shaded hours suit it best, and it sits close to other classic Stoney Point boulders.

ca_corpse_wall.blurb: The main wall at Saddle Peak, a sandstone outcrop high on the Santa Monica ridgeline above Malibu and Topanga. Roughly two dozen routes mix bolted lines with gear-protected ones, so a small rack is useful even on some bolted pitches. Grades run from easy 5.4 and 5.6 climbs up through a good spread of 5.8 to 5.10, with a handful of 5.11s and a couple of boulder problems. The wall faces north, which makes it cold and shady in winter and sunny and hot in summer; cool spring days and mild fall or winter days are best. Wind is common. The pebbly, gritty sandstone is soft, and a dry day matters.
ca_corpse_wall.parking_note: Use the lot at the Topanga Lookout trailhead, where Stunt Road meets Saddle Peak Road and Schueren Road. The Backbone Trail starts a short distance down Stunt Road from there.
ca_corpse_wall.approach: Take the Backbone Trail west and pass the water tank, then continue along the wider track. At the fork, bear right and descend to reach the base of the wall; the left branch leads to the top. Watch for poison oak near the junction.

ca_planetarium_gecko_wall.blurb: A steep sport wall in Scheelite Canyon, a side drainage of Pine Creek Canyon above Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, at about 7,250 feet. Around 27 mostly bolted single-pitch routes concentrate in the harder grades: a few 5.10s and 5.11s, then mostly 5.12 and 5.13, making this one of the densest collections of 5.12s in the canyon. The climbing is pumpy and technical, with sidepulls and laybacking on solid granite, and routes are about 60 to 90 feet long. A creek crossing on the way in is usually easy but can be tricky in high spring runoff. It tends to be quieter than many California crags.
ca_planetarium_gecko_wall.approach: Hike in from the Sheila area to the base of the wall, which begins just past the Pratt's Crack area. The route crosses the creek, usually a simple step but harder when spring runoff is high.

ca_buttress_of_cracks_left_side.blurb: The left-hand section of the Buttress of Cracks on Suicide Rock, a granite crag above Idyllwild in the San Jacinto Mountains at about 6,000 feet. Around 26 routes here are almost all traditional, with one aid line. The mix is moderate cracks, thin runout faces, hard cracks and a bold arete. Grades start near 5.8, bunch up at 5.10 and 5.11, and reach into 5.12 and 5.13 at the top end. Routes are typically one or two pitches. The surrounding rock can be polished and slick, and even bolted lines can be serious to lead, so it suits experienced trad climbers.
ca_buttress_of_cracks_left_side.approach: The main trail reaches the cliff at the Buttress of Cracks, toward its right-hand end. From there, turn left and follow the trail along the base of the wall to reach this section.
